title: Telecom fiber boom vs AI data center boom

then.summary: Late-1990s telecom carriers built out fiber and switching capacity ahead of demand. US business spending on communications equipment peaked at about 1.2% of GDP in 2000 before the bust.

now.summary: In 2025 Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta spent about $376 billion on capex, roughly 1.22% of US GDP, and Apollo cites consensus forecasts of hyperscaler capex near 3% of GDP in 2027 to 2029.

thesis: Both booms front-load physical capacity on forecasts of exploding demand; the AI build is concentrated in a handful of very large companies, while the telecom build was spread across many carriers.

sources.title: Yield Theory: AI Spending vs the Dot-Com Bubble
Apollo: The AI Capex Boom Is Building Twice as Fast as the Housing Boom

title: Railway Mania vs the AI infrastructure race

then.summary: Britain's 1840s Railway Mania was an investment disaster for many shareholders but left a national network. Railway capital formation reached nearly 7% of GDP in 1847, with Mitchell estimating 5.7% in 1846 and 6.7% in 1847.

now.summary: Kedrosky estimates AI data center capex at around 20% of the railroads' peak share of GDP and rising, already above the dot-com telecom peak.

thesis: Both are speculative financings of general-purpose networks whose public value may outlast investor losses; rails lasted a century while GPUs and data center equipment depreciate in years.

title: Cisco 2000 vs Nvidia 2025

then.summary: Cisco, the picks-and-shovels supplier of the internet build, briefly became the world's most valuable company in March 2000, then fell roughly 89% by 2002.

now.summary: Nvidia, the main supplier of AI accelerators, became the first $4 trillion and then $5 trillion company, prompting repeated comparisons of its share-price curve with Cisco's.

sources.supports: On July 9, 2025 Nvidia became the first company to reach a $4 trillion market value.

thesis: Both were the dominant equipment vendor to a capex wave and the most valuable company at its height; Nvidia's defenders point to far higher earnings and lower multiples than Cisco carried in 2000.

title: 1930s technological unemployment vs 2020s AI job fears

then.summary: With US unemployment near 20% in the Depression, Keynes named "technological unemployment" in 1930 and MIT's president argued in a 1938 article that technical progress did not mean fewer jobs.

now.summary: Employers began citing AI in layoff announcements, studies flagged weaker hiring for entry-level workers in AI-exposed jobs, and polls showed broad public worry about AI and jobs.

sources.title: Stanford SIEPR: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
sources.supports: Early-career workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations saw a 13 percent relative decline in employment.

sources.title: Challenger, Gray and Christmas: May 2026 Challenger Report
sources.supports: Employers cited AI in announced layoffs: AI led all reasons for job cuts in May 2026 (38,579 cuts) and was cited in 87,714 cuts year to date.

sources.title: Pew Research Center: U.S. Workers Are More Worried Than Hopeful About Future AI Use in the Workplace
sources.supports: Polls showed broad worry: 52% of US workers were worried about the future impact of AI in the workplace.

thesis: Both ask whether machines destroy more work than they create; the 1930s fear arrived amid mass unemployment while the 2020s fear arrived in a comparatively tight labor market.

sources.title: MIT Technology Review: People are worried that AI will take everyone's jobs. We've been here before.
Bruegel: The impact of artificial intelligence on employment

verification_note: The 1930s side is supported by MIT Technology Review. Sources for the AI-cited layoffs, the entry-level hiring study and the worker poll were added to the now side.

title: 1960s automation panic vs generative AI labor debate

then.summary: Congress held automation hearings, Time warned of automation-driven joblessness, the Triple Revolution memo predicted cybernation would break the link between work and income, and a national commission studied the question.

title: Asilomar DNA conference 1975 vs AI safety summits

then.summary: Molecular biologists paused and then set containment guidelines for recombinant DNA research at Asilomar, an influential model of scientific self-governance.

now.summary: AI researchers adopted the Asilomar AI Principles in 2017, governments convened safety summits from Bletchley Park onward, and a frontier lab proposed the option of a coordinated pause in 2026.

sources.title: Future of Life Institute: Asilomar AI Principles
sources.supports: The Asilomar AI Principles were developed at the Beneficial AI 2017 conference.

sources.title: GOV.UK: AI Safety Summit 2023, The Bletchley Declaration

sources.title: Shumaker: Anthropic's Call for a Global AI Pause
sources.supports: On June 4, 2026, Anthropic proposed that the world have the option of a globally coordinated pause or slowdown in frontier AI development.

thesis: Both cases show researchers trying to set norms for a powerful technology before law catches up; Asilomar involved a small academic field and a narrow lab hazard, while AI is a commercial, global, and dual-use industry.

title: Nuclear power "too cheap to meter" vs intelligence abundance

then.summary: AEC chairman Lewis Strauss used the phrase too cheap to meter in a 1954 address to science writers. Some later argued he meant fusion, but NRC historians conclude it was a prediction of a fission utopia, made in his personal capacity.

now.summary: Sam Altman's "The Gentle Singularity" (June 2025) argued that intelligence and energy would become wildly abundant in the 2030s, while per-token model prices fell steeply.

thesis: Both promise a foundational input so cheap it stops being metered; nuclear power never reached that point because of capital and safety costs, whereas AI token prices have fallen steeply while total compute spending rises.

sources.title: NRC: Too Cheap to Meter, A History of the Phrase
Sam Altman: The Gentle Singularity (PDF copy)
Developers Digest: What happens when tokens are too cheap to meter

verification_note: The THEN claim that NRC historians note he may have meant fusion is contradicted: the NRC article reports the fusion argument but concludes "'Too cheap to meter' was a prediction for a fission utopia in the foreseeable future. But Strauss was speaking for himself." Gentle Singularity (June 2025, wildly abundant in the 2030s) and falling token prices are supported.

title: First AI winter vs the 2025 to 2026 bubble debate

then.summary: After bold predictions, the Lighthill Report and DARPA cutbacks ended much funding for AI research in the mid-1970s, the first of several AI winters.

now.summary: Executives and investors openly debated whether AI valuations and capex were a bubble, and AI worries fed a global tech sell-off in October 2026.

thesis: Both moments pit sweeping capability claims against funders' patience; the 1970s winter was a cut in government research grants, while today's risk sits in private markets and corporate balance sheets with products already earning revenue.

title: Expert systems boom and bust vs the agent boom

then.summary: Corporations adopted rule-based expert systems after XCON paid off at DEC, then specialized Lisp machine makers collapsed in 1987 as cheaper workstations caught up and the systems proved brittle.

now.summary: Labs and software firms shipped autonomous agents and enterprises rushed to deploy them, while Gartner described a shift from generative AI hype toward foundational, responsible scaling.

thesis: Both booms sold business automation built on a new way of computing and a specialized hardware stack; whether agents avoid the brittleness and maintenance costs that sank expert systems remains untested at scale.

title: 1920s radio chaos vs AI rulemaking

then.summary: Under the 1912 law, regulators could only issue licenses and could not stop stations from interfering with each other; the Radio Act of 1927 created a commission to allocate frequencies, later replaced by the FCC.

now.summary: The EU enacted the AI Act while US states passed their own AI laws; the Senate struck a proposed federal moratorium on state AI rules 99 to 1 in July 2025, and the White House later pushed federal preemption.

thesis: In both cases a rapidly growing medium outran a weak legal framework and a fight over federal versus fragmented control followed; radio's problem was a scarce physical resource, whereas AI rules concern conduct and risk rather than allocation.

then.summary: Warnings that the millennium date bug could crash phone, power, and payment systems drove a large remediation effort, and failures in January 2000 proved far less severe than feared.

now.summary: Researchers and executives signed statements ranking AI extinction risk alongside pandemics and nuclear war, and some labs and commentators proposed pauses.

title: Manhattan Project vs the AGI race

then.summary: Japan spent more than $400 million on its Fifth Generation project, which ended in 1992 short of many goals, and DARPA's Strategic Computing program spent more than $1 billion before fading in the early 1990s.

now.summary: China, the United States, and others issued national AI strategies, laws, and infrastructure programs aimed at leadership in AI.

thesis: Each era saw governments set national targets to lead in AI out of rivalry; the 1980s programs bet on logic-based machines that the market bypassed, while today's plans largely subsidize an approach industry already leads.

title: Perceptron press hype vs ChatGPT hype

now.summary: ChatGPT's launch and claims of "sparks" of general intelligence in GPT-4 set off a new wave of coverage about thinking machines.

title: ELIZA effect vs LaMDA sentience claims

then.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA, a simple pattern-matching program, convinced some users they were understood, a tendency later named the ELIZA effect.

now.summary: In 2022 Google engineer Blake Lemoine was placed on leave after claiming the LaMDA model was sentient, while companion chatbots drew millions of emotionally attached users.

thesis: Both show people attributing minds to fluent text; ELIZA's tricks were trivially simple, whereas modern models are fluent enough that even experts disagree about what to call their abilities.

title: Nuclear setbacks vs the AI-driven nuclear revival

then.summary: The 1979 Three Mile Island accident, the worst in US commercial nuclear history, and later disasters slowed new reactor construction for decades.

now.summary: Constellation agreed to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 and sell all its output to Microsoft for data centers, and Google, Amazon, and Meta signed nuclear and small modular reactor deals.

thesis: The same site that symbolized nuclear fear became a symbol of AI's power hunger; the revival is driven by private buyers seeking firm carbon-free power rather than the state programs that built the first fleet.

title: Unsafe at Any Speed vs chatbot product liability

then.summary: Ralph Nader's 1965 book argued that automakers designed in dangers and blamed drivers; within a year Congress passed federal vehicle safety standards and created what became NHTSA.

now.summary: Families sued chatbot companies alleging their products harmed teenagers, states opened investigations and lawsuits, and Character.AI barred minors from open-ended chat.

thesis: Both shift blame for harm from the user to the product's design; car safety had measurable crash data and a clear regulator, while chatbot harms are harder to quantify and no dedicated agency exists.

title: Movie and comics panics vs AI companions and kids

then.summary: Studies of movies' effects on children fed film censorship in the 1930s, and 1950s fears that comics corrupted youth led to Senate hearings, comic burnings, and the industry's Comics Code.

now.summary: Concern about chatbots and social media harming teenagers produced lawsuits, age restrictions, and calls for bans.

thesis: Each new medium aimed at the young triggers alarm and industry self-regulation under pressure; past panics often overstated harm, while chatbots are interactive and personalized in ways comics and films were not.

title: War of the Worlds vs deepfakes

then.summary: Orson Welles's 1938 radio adaptation of The War of the Worlds, scripted by Howard Koch, was staged to sound like live news; later research found that reports of nationwide mass hysteria were greatly exaggerated by newspapers.

now.summary: Synthetic video, images, and voice clones were used in hoaxes such as a fake Pentagon explosion image and a fake Biden robocall.

then.summary: Napster made free music file sharing mainstream until a 2001 federal court ruling held it liable for copyright infringement, after which licensed digital music services emerged.

now.summary: Publishers, image libraries, and authors sued AI companies over training on copyrighted works, and Anthropic agreed to a $1.5 billion settlement with authors in 2025.

thesis: Both pit a new distribution or production technology against rights holders, with courts and licensing deals shaping the business model; AI firms argue training is transformative fair use, a defense unavailable to a pure copying service.

now.summary: Releases of powerful open-weight models prompted debate over whether governments should restrict publishing model weights on security grounds.

title: The dynamo productivity lag vs AI productivity

then.summary: Economist Paul David argued in 1990 that factory electrification took decades to raise productivity because plants had to be redesigned around the new power source, and used the case to explain Solow's computer paradox.

now.summary: Generative AI reached hundreds of millions of users quickly while measured economy-wide productivity effects remained debated.

thesis: General-purpose technologies tend to show up in productivity statistics only after organizations are rebuilt around them; AI may diffuse faster because it runs on existing devices, but the organizational redesign is the same bottleneck.

title: 1970 AGI predictions vs 2020s AGI timelines

then.summary: Marvin Minsky told Life magazine in 1970 that "in from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being," and Herbert Simon had made a twenty-year prediction of human-level machine capability in 1965.

now.summary: Essays and scenarios from researchers and lab leaders forecast AGI or superintelligence within a few years.

thesis: Both generations of forecasters extrapolated recent breakthroughs to human-level AI within a decade; the 1970 claims rested on toy demonstrations, while today's rest on measured benchmark and compute trends that may not continue.

title: CFCs and the Montreal Protocol vs an AI treaty

then.summary: Chlorofluorocarbons, introduced around 1930 as safe refrigerants, were found to destroy stratospheric ozone, and in 1987 governments agreed to phase them out on a binding schedule.

now.summary: The Council of Europe adopted the first binding international AI convention, and advocates have proposed Montreal Protocol style regimes with phased, verifiable commitments for advanced AI.

thesis: Both cases ask nations to constrain a profitable, widely used technology on the basis of scientific warnings; CFCs had ready substitutes and a measurable harm, while AI has neither a drop-in substitute nor agreed metrics.
